Chapter 9: The Relationship Between Medium, Message, and Audience.
Comics aren’t created in isolation. There’s this lively back-and-forth between the medium, the message, and you—the audience. Every comic is shaped by the world it comes from: the culture, the technology, and, just as importantly, what readers are hoping to find.
Now, the medium of comics—it sets the stage, but it also draws the boundaries. Think about the size and shape of a comic page, or whether you’re flipping through print or scrolling on your phone. Every format and genre has its own set of rules. So, creators have to get clever, working within those limits to bring their stories to life.
The message—the heart of the story or idea—gets sculpted by those same boundaries. Some tales just belong in the world of comics, where pictures and words dance together to show emotion, subtlety, or even complexity you might not get in a novel or a movie. Other stories might work better in a different medium altogether.
Here are a few things that shape this relationship:
First, cultural context. Different societies see and understand visual storytelling in their own ways. What feels familiar in one place could seem totally new somewhere else.
Then, there’s technology. Digital tools, webcomics, and new ways of sharing stories have totally changed the comic landscape, opening doors for both creators and readers.
And of course, reader expectations. We all bring our own experiences, our favorite genres, and even our personal histories to the table when we pick up a comic. That shapes how we see the story.
Here’s something fascinating: The audience isn’t just along for the ride. You actually help create meaning. Your background, your assumptions, your imagination—they all shape the story you experience. The same comic can feel completely different depending on who's reading it, or even when it’s read.
This ever-changing relationship is what keeps comics so fresh and exciting. It’s why the medium keeps growing and adapting, always ready to meet new ideas, new technology, and new readers—like you.
